newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Waigel says Germany to make EMU goals.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Waigel says Germany to make EMU goals.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Tuesday he would ensure Germany meets the tough criteria for European monetary union (EMU) in 1997, despite leading research institutes' forecast that it would miss the targets.

The six economic think tanks said Germany's economy was strengthening but that its 1997 budget deficit would be 3.5 percent of economic output, above the 3.0-percent "reference value" in the Maastricht Treaty. They also predicted Germany's outstanding debt would slightly exceed the 60-percent target.

But Waigel said "The federal government will continue its strict consolidation course. It will create the conditions so that the 1997 deficit lies below three percent of gross domestic product (GDP). The necessary decisions will be met in the final negotiations over the 1997 budget."
Parliament's budget committee meets on November 14 to work out a final draft budget for 1997 before submitting it for parliamentary approval.
1997 is the key year for deciding which countries will participate in EMU at the scheduled start in January 1999.

But Waigel, who with Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer have been among the most strident voices in Europe that criteria be strictly interpreted to ensure the euro stays at least as stable as the German mark, is running out of time.
Recently, the Free Democrats, junior partners in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition, stood in the way of increasing taxes to plug the widening holes in state finances.
Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Koebnick, in London, conceded that Germany might miss the Maastricht targets but added that they could be interpreted flexibly.
However, he said a deviation of more than 10 percent from the prescribed deficit ratio would not be acceptable. "3.3 percent is too much," he said.
Despite the expected overshoot in the budget deficit, the institutes still expected EMU to happen.

In its semi-annual report, which serves as a reference for the government and does not necessarily influence policy, the institutes said hitting the targets at the beginning of European monetary union was less important than continued stability after the start.

"We assume that EMU will happen," chief economist Werner Schatz of the Kiel-based Institute of the World Economy (IfW), one of the six, told a news conference. "The (Maastricht) treaty allows for the possibility that the criteria will not be precisely met.
"What's important is a commitment to stability, with sanctions, for the period after the start," Schatz said.
Financial sector analysts also said Waigel would probably not hit the target but that Germany would surely be in the first wave of countries to launch the euro currency.

"Discussions over a strict interpretation of the Maastricht criteria (will become) more sensitive. Monetary union certainly can't start without Germany," said Karen Kricks-Brunnlieb, head of bond analysis at Trinkaus & Burkhardt.

The six institutes also said German GDP was likely to grow 1.5 percent in 1996, rising to 2.5 percent growth in 1997. The 1996 projection was up from a forecast of 0.75-percent growth made by the same institutes six months ago.
The institutes said the current level of interest rates is appropriate, but a slight tightening is possible if M3 money supply growth remains above target levels.

The Bundesbank should also not hesitate to raise interest rates slightly if M3 remains above target. A slight tightening to bring M3 back into the target corridor would pose no danger of ending the economic upturn, the report said.
Unemployment was forecast to remain high at 10.4 percent in 1997, up from 10.3 percent in 1996 and 9.4 percent in 1995, the institutes said.
Meanwhile, consumer price inflation was seen remaining subdued at 1.5 percent next year, unchanged from this year and down from 1.8 percent in 1995.
